title: Festivals and Faiths
description: Ten calm, respectful texts about how communities celebrate: Diwali in a New Jersey town, a Passover Seder, Ramadan evenings, a doctor's advice on fasting, a Christmas market, Lunar New Year, the real history of Thanksgiving, the Day of the Dead, an interfaith dinner and a walk on the Camino de Santiago.

lessons.title: Lights Over Oak Tree Road
lessons.summary: A New Jersey town celebrates Diwali, its fireworks show is postponed by rain, and a fireworks expert explains how the colors are made.
lessons.text:
Every autumn, the town of Edison, New Jersey, glows a little brighter than usual. Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated here by thousands of families with roots in India, and for a week the shops along Oak Tree Road hang strings of lights and sell boxes of sweets almost faster than they can fill them.

Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, and each community gives the festival its own meaning. For many Hindus, it marks the return of Lord Rama to his city after fourteen years in exile, when the people lit rows of lamps to welcome him home. Families clean their houses, wear new clothes, draw colorful patterns at their doors and light small clay lamps, and many honor Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth.

Priya Mehta, a longtime resident who came to Edison as a young bride more than forty years ago, remembers when the whole celebration fit into a rented hall. "Now the temple on our street is the nucleus of the neighborhood," she says. "Everything grows out from it, the way a cell is built around its nucleus." Like many longtime residents, she has watched a few families become a town within a town.

The public celebration ends each year with a fireworks show in a park. A town ordinance does not allow residents to set off large fireworks on their own, so the town hires a licensed company. The ordinance exists for a good reason: fireworks are exceptionally dangerous in the wrong hands.

This year, heavy rain on Saturday meant the show was postponed until Sunday night. Some children were disappointed, but most parents agreed that a postponed show was better than a dangerous one.

While the crew waited, its leader, Dev Shah, explained how fireworks work. Each shell contains black powder, a potent mixture that burns in an instant. A first charge propels the shell high into the air, and a second charge bursts it open. "The powder is volatile," Shah said, "so we keep it in locked steel boxes, far from any flame. Volatile materials do not forgive mistakes."

The colors come from metals. Copper gives blue, and copper oxide, a compound of copper and oxygen, is one common source of it. Blue is exceptionally hard to produce, because the flame must be hot enough to bring out the color but not so hot that it washes the color away.

On Sunday the sky was clear. One shell after another was propelled into the dark, and when the first deep blue burst opened above the park, a cheer rose from the crowd. Priya Mehta was there with her grandchildren. "The lamps are the real heart of Diwali," she said, "but I will not pretend I don't love this part too."

Questions:
Why was the fireworks show postponed?
Because of heavy rain on Saturday, it was postponed until Sunday night.
What does the town ordinance say about fireworks?
The ordinance does not allow residents to set off large fireworks on their own, so the town hires a licensed company.
What propels a firework shell into the air?
A first charge of black powder, a potent mixture, propels the shell into the air.
Where does the blue color in fireworks come from?
It comes from copper, and copper oxide is one common source of it.
What does Priya Mehta call the temple on her street?
She calls it the nucleus of the neighborhood, because everything grows out from it.

lessons.title: A Seat at the Seder
lessons.summary: A guest attends her first Passover Seder with a colleague's family in Philadelphia and learns what each part of the evening means.
lessons.text:
When my colleague Rachel Adler invited me to her family's Passover Seder, I accepted at once and then worried for a week that I would do something wrong. "It's understandable to be nervous," she told me, "but a Seder is made for questions."

Passover is the Jewish festival that remembers the Exodus, the story of how the Israelites, who had been slaves in Egypt, were led to freedom. The Seder is the special meal held on its first night. The word Seder means "order," and the order of the evening has stayed largely unchanged for centuries: the same blessings, the same foods and the same story, read from a book called the Haggadah.

There were twelve of us at her parents' table in Philadelphia. First came the flat bread called matzah. The Israelites left Egypt in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise, so during the eight days of Passover many Jewish families eat no ordinary bread. The matzah was dry and thin, and it began to crumble as soon as I broke it. By the end of the night, the table was covered in pieces, and nobody minded the crumbling at all.

The youngest child, Rachel's nephew Sam, who is eight, asked the Four Questions in Hebrew. He had been learning the Hebrew alphabet for two years, and he read slowly, his finger moving from right to left, the direction in which that alphabet is written. The questions begin by asking why this night is different from all other nights.

Later we were told to sit comfortably and lean on cushions. Slaves ate standing and in a hurry; free people may eat comfortably. Rachel's father told the story of the ten plagues, and of how the sea opened for the Israelites and then closed over Pharaoh's army, which drowned. At each plague, everyone removed a drop of wine from their cup. Rachel explained that a cup of joy cannot be full while others suffer, even the soldiers who drowned while chasing the Israelites.

The children then performed a short roleplay of the escape, with towels for robes and a blue sheet for the sea. Sam's older sister called the roleplay childish, but she still played Moses. "Tonight, childish is allowed," her grandmother said. The grandmother had also made the fish course from pike, with a recipe unchanged since her own mother's time, and she told me that fresh pike is the secret.

Near the end of the meal, a piece of matzah was hidden, and the children hunted for it. Sam found it within a minute but pretended he had not. It was a bluff: by custom, the child who finds it may ask for a small prize before giving it back, and Sam's bluff earned him a new book. My week of worry had been understandable, but by the end of the night I felt like one of the family.

Questions:
Why does the matzah crumble so easily?
It is dry, thin bread made without time to rise, because the Israelites left Egypt in a hurry.
Why does everyone sit comfortably and lean on cushions?
Slaves ate standing and in a hurry, but free people may eat comfortably.
Why does everyone remove a drop of wine for each plague?
A cup of joy cannot be full while others suffer, even the soldiers who drowned.
How did Sam use a bluff?
He pretended he had not found the matzah, so that he could ask for a small prize.

lessons.title: The Courier's Iftar
lessons.summary: A bicycle courier in Minneapolis fasts during Ramadan, delivers food all afternoon and breaks his fast at sunset with his family.
lessons.text:
Yusuf Ali has worked as a bicycle courier in Minneapolis for six years. Most of what he carries is food: lunches, coffees and cakes for office meetings. For most of the year, that is simply a courier's job. During Ramadan, it becomes something of a test.

Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Each day, from the first light of dawn until sunset, Muslims who are healthy enough take no food and no water. The fast is meant to teach patience and self-control, to remind people of those who are hungry and to bring them closer to God. The evenings are as important as the days: families and friends gather to break the fast together, at a meal called iftar.

Ironically, Yusuf's busiest hours fall in the late afternoon, when he is hungriest. He spends them carrying warm sandwiches and iced drinks to other people. "It sounds hard," he says, "but ironically, it helps. Every delivery reminds me why I am fasting." The craving that troubles him most is not for food at all. It is for water. By four o'clock, the craving for one cold glass is stronger than any hunger.

Because the Islamic calendar follows the moon, Ramadan begins about eleven days earlier each year and slowly moves through all the seasons. When it falls in summer in the northern hemisphere, a fast in Minneapolis can last more than sixteen hours. Yusuf's cousin lives in Melbourne, in the southern hemisphere, where at the same time of year the days are short and the fast ends in the early evening. The cousins compare sunset times by video call and joke about which hemisphere has the better deal.

Yusuf checks the exact time of sunset on his cellphone, which has an app that lists the times of prayer. When his cellphone battery dies or he goes offline in a building with no signal, he relies on a paper timetable from his mosque, folded in his jacket.

At sunset, he tries to be home with his family. The street outside is loud, and the traffic would drown the call to prayer from the mosque, so his little sister plays it on her phone, loud enough to drown out the street. They break the fast with dates, the sweet fruit, and water, then pray together. After that comes the meal: lentil soup, rice with spiced chicken and a cold drink of yogurt mixed with water and mint. The yogurt drink is his favorite part.

At the end of the month comes Eid al-Fitr, a festival of prayer, new clothes, gifts and visits. Yusuf will give money to a local food bank, as many families do. The month is hard, he says, but it is worthwhile. "I notice things I usually rush past," he says. "That alone makes it worthwhile."

Questions:
Why is the late afternoon hard for the courier during Ramadan?
It is his busiest time, and he is hungry while he carries food and drinks to other people.
What is his strongest craving during the fast?
His strongest craving is for a glass of cold water.
Why does Ramadan move through the seasons?
The Islamic calendar follows the moon, so Ramadan begins about eleven days earlier each year.
What does Yusuf do when he goes offline?
He uses a paper timetable from his mosque.
How does the family break the fast?
They break the fast with dates and water, pray together and then eat the meal.

lessons.title: The Doctor Before Ramadan
lessons.summary: In an interview, a family doctor in Michigan explains how she helps her patients decide whether and how to fast safely during Ramadan.
lessons.text:
Every year, a few weeks before Ramadan, Dr. Hana Malik gives a talk at a community center in Dearborn, Michigan, about fasting safely. She is a family doctor and a Muslim who fasts herself. We asked her what patients most want to know.

What is the most common question?
"Whether they should fast at all. Islam itself treats health as paramount. People who are ill or on a journey, pregnant women and the very old are not required to fast. They can make up the days later or, if they cannot, help feed a person in need for each day they miss. So the duty is already waived for people it would harm. My job is to help each patient see whether it is waived for them."

Is there a stigma attached to not fasting?
"Sometimes. Some patients are afraid people will judge them for eating. I understand that fear, but taking the exemption is following the rules, not breaking them. When religious leaders say so from the front of the mosque, the stigma begins to fade."

Who should not fast?
"Anyone having chemotherapy, for example. Chemotherapy is hard on the body, and patients need water and regular meals. The same goes for someone with a serious bacterial infection who needs antibiotics every six or eight hours. A bacterial infection does not wait for sunset."

What about long-term conditions?
"Many people can fast safely with planning. Take high cholesterol. Fasting itself is rarely the problem; the problem is a heavy, fried meal at sunset. When patients break the fast with fruit, soup and grilled food, their cholesterol often stays the same or even improves.

"Asthma brings another question: does an inhaler break the fast? Scholars give different answers, and I am not a religious scholar, so I send patients to their imam for that part. As a doctor, I can often move their asthma medicine to doses taken before dawn and after sunset."

And other conditions?
"Some patients live with inflammation of the joints. Others have systemic inflammation, which affects the whole body rather than one joint. Their pills can usually be moved to the morning and evening meals, but with a systemic illness I want to see the patient before Ramadan, not after a problem."

What about vaccination?
"Many scholars say that an injection which is not food does not break the fast, so a vaccination is usually possible, though some patients choose to have a vaccination after sunset."

Do patients ever worry too much?
"Some feel almost paranoid that brushing their teeth or having a blood test will spoil their fast. I tell them they are not paranoid, only careful, and careful is good. A doctor and an imam, working together, can usually put their minds at rest."

Questions:
Why does Dr. Malik say the duty to fast is waived for some people?
Islam treats health as paramount, so people who are ill or on a journey, pregnant women and the very old are not required to fast.
Why should a patient having chemotherapy not fast?
Chemotherapy is hard on the body, and the patient needs water and regular meals.
How can people with high cholesterol fast safely?
They should break the fast with fruit, soup and grilled food instead of a heavy, fried meal.
What is the difference between inflammation of one joint and systemic inflammation?
Systemic inflammation affects the whole body rather than one joint.

lessons.title: A Christmas Market Under the Castle
lessons.summary: A woman visits the Christmas market in Edinburgh with her Scottish mother-in-law and young daughter and learns where such markets came from.
lessons.text:
My husband's mother, Morag, has a rule: the first Saturday of December belongs to the Christmas market. So on a cold, bright afternoon, she, my four-year-old daughter Ella and I walked down into the gardens below Edinburgh Castle, where rows of wooden huts sold hot drinks, sausages, candles and toys under strings of white lights.

High above us, the castle sat on its black rock. Morag told Ella that for centuries soldiers had lived up there as a garrison, guarding the city. "A garrison is soldiers who live in a fort," she said, "and that castle had a garrison of one kind or another for hundreds of years." Ella looked up, clearly hoping to see a soldier.

Markets like this one are not originally Scottish. Their emergence goes back to the late Middle Ages in German-speaking towns, where people gathered in the weeks before Christmas to buy food and supplies for the winter. A market in Vienna is recorded in 1298, and the famous market in Dresden dates from 1434. Over time, the markets became part of the season itself, with toys, sweets and decorations. Their eventual spread to Britain and America came much later, and the Edinburgh market is quite young. Still, the old tradition seems at home here, and its eventual success in Scotland is easy to understand.

For Christians, Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus, and many of the stalls reflected that. One sold figures carved by hand in the mountains of eastern Germany: angels, shepherds and a small madonna, a figure of Mary holding the baby Jesus. The woman at the stall told me that her father had carved a madonna like it every winter for forty years. I bought one for Morag, who has kept a madonna by her window all her life.

Near the end of one row, a fence made a small enclosure with straw on the ground, where two sheep and a donkey stood beside a wooden stable. The sheep slept, but the donkey pushed its nose over the edge of the enclosure toward every passing child. It was clearly the scene stealer of the whole market. "Every year there is one scene stealer," Morag said, "and it is never the one you expect."

As the light faded, a choir gathered on the steps of a nearby church and began a Gloria, an old hymn of praise that is sung in many churches at Christmas. People stopped walking to listen. Ella, who did not know the words, swayed in time, and when the Gloria ended she clapped louder than anyone.

"Isn't she bonny?" said Morag. In Scotland, bonny means pretty or lovely. A woman next to us smiled and agreed that she was very bonny indeed.

Questions:
What is a garrison, according to Morag?
A garrison is a group of soldiers who live in a fort.
Where did the emergence of Christmas markets begin?
It began in the late Middle Ages in German-speaking towns.
What did the writer buy for Morag?
She bought a small madonna, a figure of Mary holding the baby Jesus.
Why was the donkey the scene stealer?
It pushed its nose over the edge of the enclosure toward every passing child.
What does bonny mean in Scotland?
It means pretty or lovely.

lessons.title: Home for the New Year
lessons.summary: A young doctor takes two days off from her hospital in Boston to spend Lunar New Year with her family in Queens.
lessons.text:
Mei Wong is in the second year of her residency at a hospital in Boston, which means she works long nights and rarely has a free weekend. But every winter she asks for two days off, because nothing is allowed to keep her from Lunar New Year with her family in Queens, New York.

Lunar New Year, also called the Spring Festival, follows the old lunar calendar, so it falls on a different day each year, somewhere between late January and the middle of February. It is the most important holiday of the year in China, and it is also celebrated in Vietnam, Korea and by communities all over the world.

Mei took the train to New York with a yen for one thing above all: her grandmother's dumplings. When she arrived, the apartment was perfectly clean. Before the New Year, families clean their homes from top to bottom to sweep away the bad luck of the old year. Her father had even climbed a ladder to clean the air duct above the stove. "No dust in the duct, no dust in the new year," he said.

On the wall by the door hung her grandmother's motto, written in black ink on red paper: family first, then everything else. Mei had grown up with that motto, and at that moment she understood it better than ever.

On the eve of the New Year, the whole family gathered for the reunion dinner, the most important meal of the holiday. There was a whole fish, because in Chinese the word for fish sounds like the word for plenty. There were long noodles for a long life and, at last, dumplings shaped like the gold and silver money of old China.

Over dinner, her grandmother told the children the story of Nian, a monster that came out of the sea or the mountains each New Year to attack the villages. One year the people discovered that Nian was frightened of the color red, of fire and of loud noise. So they hung red paper on their doors and lit firecrackers, and the frightened monster ran away. That, she said, is why the holiday is so red and so loud.

Her grandmother was born in a Year of the Rabbit, one of the twelve animals of the Chinese calendar, and she has always loved the old tale of the jade hare, a gentle white hare that lives on the moon and makes medicine there.

After dinner, the elders gave the children red envelopes with money inside. Mei's young cousin showed their grandmother how to send a red envelope by phone, using the app's scanner to read a code, but the grandmother found the scanner too complicated and gave out paper envelopes instead. Mei, a millennial who pays for everything with her phone, secretly agreed with her. Some things, even for a millennial, should still be paper.

Questions:
Why does Mei rarely have a free weekend?
She is in the second year of her residency at a hospital, so she works long nights.
What did Mei have a yen for?
She had a yen for her grandmother's dumplings.
Why did her father clean the air duct?
Families clean their homes before the New Year to sweep away the bad luck of the old year.
What was Nian frightened of?
Nian was frightened of the color red, of fire and of loud noise.
Why did the grandmother give out paper envelopes?
She found the scanner on the phone too complicated.

lessons.title: What We Know About the First Thanksgiving
lessons.summary: A history teacher explains in a column what the sources really say about the harvest meal of 1621 and how Thanksgiving later became a national holiday.
lessons.text:
Every November, my students arrive with the same picture in their heads: men in black hats, a long table, a roast turkey and pumpkin pie. I teach history, and each year I ask them to put that picture under scrutiny. Historians are not oracles. We cannot see the past directly; we can only read what people wrote at the time. So here is what the sources tell us.

Firstly, the people. In 1620, about one hundred English passengers arrived on the Mayflower and built a settlement at Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts. Many of them had left England so that they could worship in their own way. They did not call themselves the Pilgrims. Their leader, William Bradford, once wrote that they knew they were pilgrims, people passing through this world, but the name became common only about two hundred years later.

The land was not empty. It was the home of the Wampanoag people, who had lived there for thousands of years and who had recently lost many lives to disease brought by European sailors. In 1621, their leader, Massasoit, made an agreement with the newcomers, and a Wampanoag man named Tisquantum, who spoke English, showed them how to grow corn.

Secondly, the meal. That autumn, after the harvest, the English held a celebration that lasted about three days. Only one account by someone who was there survives, a short letter by a settler named Edward Winslow. He says the men hunted birds, and that Massasoit came with about ninety men, who killed five deer and gave them to the settlers. Turkey may have been eaten, but the letter does not say so. There were no pies, because there were no ovens to bake them. Lobster, however, was so common in the bay that it may well have been on the table. As for popcorn, the popular story that the Wampanoag brought popcorn first appears in books written more than 250 years later, and no evidence from the time supports it.

Finally, the holiday. For a long time, Thanksgiving was a local custom. Its national form owes much to Sarah Josepha Hale, a magazine editor who led a crusade of letters and articles for seventeen years, asking presidents to create a national day of thanks. Her crusade succeeded in 1863, during the Civil War, a time of deep instability, when Abraham Lincoln called on the whole country to give thanks together. Amid such instability, a shared day of thanks meant a great deal.

The story does not end there. Since 1970, some Native Americans have gathered at Plymouth on Thanksgiving for a National Day of Mourning, to remember what the arrival of the settlers cost their peoples. Many families, meanwhile, rightly treasure the day as a time of gratitude. Under scrutiny, the old picture changes, and a careful history class, I think, rightly leaves room for both.

Questions:
Why are historians not oracles?
They cannot see the past directly; they can only read what people wrote at the time.
What is the teacher's first point?
Firstly, the teacher writes about the people: the English settlers and the Wampanoag.
Why might lobster have been on the table?
Lobster was very common in the bay at that time.
What is the problem with the story about popcorn?
It first appears in books written more than 250 years later, and no evidence from the time supports it.
What was Sarah Josepha Hale's crusade?
She wrote letters and articles for seventeen years, asking presidents to create a national day of thanks.

lessons.title: An Altar for Grandpa Luis
lessons.summary: A mother and son in San Antonio prepare an altar for the Day of the Dead and spend the evening at the cemetery remembering his grandfather.
lessons.text:
Every year at the end of October, Elena Morales clears the low table in her living room in San Antonio, Texas, and her son Mateo, who is ten, knows what that means. It is time to build the altar for the Day of the Dead.

The Day of the Dead is celebrated mainly on November 1 and 2, in Mexico and by Mexican families everywhere. It is not a sad holiday, and it is not a Mexican Halloween. Many families believe that for these two days the souls of the dead come home to visit, and they prepare a welcome: an altar with photographs, candles, water, salt and the favorite foods of the people they have lost.

This year Mateo's job was the bread. He and his mother walked to the bakery on their corner. The bakery makes pan de muerto, the bread of the dead, only at this time of year: a round, sweet loaf decorated on top with strips of dough shaped like bones and covered in sugar.

On the altar they placed a photograph of Elena's father, Luis, who died three years ago, along with his favorite candy and a cup of coffee. Around everything they laid orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are said to guide the dead home.

As they worked, Elena explained where the holiday comes from. Long before the Spanish arrived, the native peoples of Mexico held festivals to honor their dead. Spanish clergy brought the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, on November 1 and 2, and over time the two traditions blended. Some of the clergy tried to end the old customs, but they survived inside the new ones.

She also showed Mateo a drawing of La Catrina, an elegant skeleton in a huge hat covered with flowers. The artist José Guadalupe Posada first drew her more than a century ago to make fun of people who were vain about their wealth and copied European fashion. His skeletons show a gentle contempt for the vain and for greed, not contempt for death. Rich or poor, they say, we all end as bones, and greed cannot change that.

On the evening of November 2, they drove to the cemetery, a quiet field enclosed by a low stone wall. Inside the enclosed ground, families had cleaned the graves, lit candles and set out food and music. Mateo's aunt had painted his face like a skull, but the white paint left a smear on his collar, and the black paint around his eyes became a smear down his cheek when he laughed.

They sat by Luis's grave until late, and Elena told stories about him that Mateo had heard before. That, she said, was the point. Every year the family would revisit the same stories, and each time they revisited them, Luis would come home a little.

Questions:
What does the bakery make only at this time of year?
It makes pan de muerto, a round, sweet bread decorated with shapes like bones.
Why do families place marigolds on the altar?
Their bright color and strong scent are said to guide the dead home.
What did the Spanish clergy bring to Mexico?
They brought the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, on November 1 and 2.
Why did Posada create La Catrina?
He wanted to make fun of people who were vain about their wealth and copied European fashion.

lessons.title: One Long Table
lessons.summary: The organizer of an interfaith dinner in an Ohio town describes how the dinner works and why it is held in a hall with a troubled history.
lessons.text:
Every spring, on a Sunday evening, about two hundred people sit down together at one long table in the old community hall on Mill Street in our town in Ohio. They are Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists, and people of no creed at all. I am a retired teacher, and for eleven years I have helped organize this dinner. People often ask how it works, so here is the answer.

The dinner is run by a council of local congregations: a synagogue, two mosques, a Catholic parish, a Hindu temple, a gurdwara, where Sikhs worship, and Pastor Daniel Ellis's evangelical church, the largest in town. We follow a simple system whereby each congregation cooks one dish, and every dish must be acceptable to every guest. That means no pork, no alcohol and plenty of vegetarian food. It is a system whereby nobody has to ask what they can eat.

The clergy do not give speeches. Instead, they serve. For one evening, the rabbi, the priest, the imams and the evangelical pastor are at the beck and call of everyone else, carrying plates, pouring water and clearing tables. Pastor Ellis says that being at the beck and call of strangers is the best lesson in being humble that he knows. The idea came partly from the Sikh tradition of the community kitchen, where people of every creed and background sit side by side and eat the same free meal.

We do invite one guest to speak briefly. Last year it was a retired philosophy professor, a thinker who has spent his life writing about how strangers learn to trust each other. The message of this gentle thinker was short: you cannot fear a person while you are passing them the bread.

Why the old hall on Mill Street? Because of its history. When the hall was built, the papers for the land on that street contained a rule of exclusion. They said that the land, or any part thereof, could never be sold to certain families because of their faith or their race. Rules of exclusion like this were once common in towns across the country. Courts made them impossible to enforce many decades ago, and today the rule is simply null and void, but the words are still there in the old papers. A null rule cannot hurt anyone now. The memory thereof, however, is worth keeping.

So each year, before dinner, a young person reads that old rule aloud, and then we all sit down together on the very land it once tried to keep from some of us. Nobody makes a speech about it. The table says enough.

Questions:
Who comes to the dinner?
Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists and people of no creed at all come to the dinner.
What is the system whereby every guest can eat every dish?
Each congregation cooks one dish, and every dish must be acceptable to every guest.
What do the clergy do at the dinner?
They are at the beck and call of everyone else, carrying plates, pouring water and clearing tables.
What did the old papers for the land say?
They said that the land, or any part thereof, could never be sold to certain families because of their faith or their race.
Why is the old rule null and void today?
Courts made such rules impossible to enforce many decades ago.

lessons.title: Five Hundred Miles to Santiago
lessons.summary: A retired aerospace engineer walks the Camino de Santiago across northern Spain and learns that the road cannot be planned like an aircraft part.
lessons.text:
For thirty-five years I worked as an engineer in the aerospace industry near Seattle. My specialty was weight. In aerospace, every extra ounce costs fuel, so my job was optimization: making each part of an aircraft as light as it could be while keeping it strong. When I retired, I decided to walk the Camino de Santiago, the old pilgrims' road across northern Spain, and I prepared for it the only way I knew, with numbers.

Since the Middle Ages, pilgrims have walked to the city of Santiago de Compostela, where, by tradition, the remains of Saint James, one of the followers of Jesus, rest in the cathedral. The most popular route begins at the foot of the Pyrenees and runs about five hundred miles west. Many people still walk it as an act of Catholic faith. Others walk for reasons they find hard to name, and the road seems to welcome both.

My pack was a project in optimization. I weighed every sock and every pen. My analytical mind was very pleased. Then, at the first hostel, a woman from Ireland lifted my pack and laughed. It was overweight, she said, by any reasonable rule: a pack should weigh no more than a tenth of the person carrying it. Mine was nearly double that. Over the next three days, I mailed home a jacket, two books and a camera. The overweight pack had taught me more than all my numbers.

At that first hostel, I also received my credentials, a folded paper booklet that every pilgrim carries. At each night's stop, someone stamps it, and at the end the stamps prove that you walked. By the second week, my credentials were full of colorful stamps from churches, cafés and hostels.

The road passed through one hamlet after another: a church, a fountain, a few stone houses and a dog asleep in the sun. In one tiny hamlet, an old man handed out figs from his tree to every pilgrim who passed, and he would not take money.

On the high, flat plain in the middle of the route, there is almost no shade for days. I wore my sunglasses from morning until evening, but my arms burned anyway, and I developed a heat rash that lasted a week. At a small pharmacy, a woman gave me a cream for the rash and told me, kindly, to buy a shirt with long sleeves and to keep my sunglasses on.

What the road tests most is endurance, not speed. My analytical habits wanted to measure my daily miles and improve them. Endurance, I learned, is mostly patience: getting up each morning and walking again.

I reached Santiago after thirty-four days. In the square before the cathedral, pilgrims from every country sat on the stones, resting. I sat among them and did not calculate anything at all.

Questions:
What was the writer's job in the aerospace industry?
His job was optimization: making each part of an aircraft as light as possible while keeping it strong.
Why was his pack overweight?
A pack should weigh no more than a tenth of the person carrying it, and his weighed nearly double that.
What are a pilgrim's credentials?
They are a folded paper booklet that is stamped at each stop to prove that the pilgrim walked.
What did the writer find in each hamlet?
He found a church, a fountain, a few stone houses and a dog asleep in the sun.
